questions.question: How do you handle errors when consuming an HTTP API in Python?
questions.title: Error Handling in HTTP API Calls
questions.direct_answer: Handle two layers: transport errors (the request fails to send — connection refused, timeout, DNS) which raise exceptions (ConnectionError, Timeout), and HTTP errors (the server responds with an error status — 4xx/5xx) which you surface with response.raise_for_status(). Check status codes explicitly for fine-grained handling (if response.status_code != 200), wrap the call in try/except for transport failures, and always set timeouts so a hung server doesn't block you forever. The pattern: try with a timeout, except transport exceptions, then raise_for_status or check the status.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you distinguish transport errors (exceptions) from HTTP errors (status codes), use raise_for_status(), and always set a timeout.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting timeouts (a hung server blocks forever), or treating a 4xx/5xx response as success because no exception was thrown.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Two layers: transport errors raise exceptions (ConnectionError, Timeout); HTTP errors need raise_for_status() or status-code checks. Always set a timeout.

sections.title: Two Layers of Errors
sections.content: Consuming an HTTP API has two error layers. Transport errors mean the request failed to send or complete — a refused connection, a timeout, a DNS failure — and these raise exceptions (requests.exceptions.ConnectionError, Timeout). HTTP errors mean the request reached the server but the server responded with an error status (4xx client error, 5xx server error); these do NOT raise by default, so you surface them with response.raise_for_status() or by checking response.status_code. Two disciplines make this robust: always pass a timeout= so a hung server doesn't block you forever, and wrap the call in try/except for the transport exceptions you can recover from (retry on Timeout, report on ConnectionError).

sections.title: Transport vs HTTP Errors
sections.content:
Transport failures raise exceptions; HTTP errors are status codes you must check.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C[requests.get\(url, timeout=10\)] -->|connection refused/timeout| E[Exception: ConnectionError/Timeout]
  C -->|response received| R{status code}
  R -->|2xx| OK[success]
  R -->|4xx/5xx| H[raise_for_status or check code]
```

sections.title: Robust error handling with requests
sections.content:
```python
import requests
from requests.exceptions import ConnectionError, Timeout, HTTPError

try:
    r = requests.get(url, timeout=10)          # ALWAYS set a timeout
    r.raise_for_status()                       # 4xx/5xx -> raises HTTPError
    data = r.json()                            # success
except Timeout:
    # transport: server didn't respond in time -> maybe retry
    ...
except ConnectionError:
    # transport: couldn't connect -> report, don't retry blindly
    ...
except HTTPError as e:
    # HTTP: server returned 4xx/5xx -> inspect e.response.status_code
    if e.response.status_code == 404: ...
    elif e.response.status_code == 429: ...   # rate limited -> back off
except ValueError:
    # r.json() failed: the body wasn't valid JSON
    ...
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Forgetting to pass a timeout — a hung server blocks the call (and your program) forever.
Treating a 4xx/5xx response as success because no exception was thrown (requests doesn't raise by default).
Not distinguishing a retryable transport error (Timeout) from a client error (404, won't fix by retrying).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Two error layers: transport (exceptions: ConnectionError, Timeout) and HTTP (status codes: 4xx/5xx).
Use response.raise_for_status() to turn a 4xx/5xx into an exception; or check status_code explicitly.
Always pass a timeout= so a hung server doesn't block forever.
Wrap the call in try/except for transport exceptions you can recover from (retry on Timeout).
Don't retry a 404 — it's a client error, not transient; do retry a 429/5xx with backoff.
